Vomit
VOM-it
n. / v.
From Latin vomere, to throw up. Webster 1828: matter ejected from the stomach; also, to eject from the stomach. Scripture uses it in two figures of great force — the dog returning to its vomit, and the land itself vomiting out its inhabitants.

Biblical Definition

Vomit is one of Scripture’s most deliberately repulsive figures, and it is used to describe two things: the false convert and the defiled land. Solomon fixes the first: As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly (Proverbs 26:11). Peter takes the proverb up, adds a second, and applies both to those who had escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of Christ and were entangled again: The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire (2 Peter 2:22). The force of the pairing is exact. Neither animal changed its nature. The dog was reformed of nothing and the sow was washed on the outside; both returned to what they were, and that is Peter’s point about the apostate. The second figure is Leviticus’s, and it is used of the land as a moral agent under God: the land is defiled: therefore I do visit the iniquity thereof upon it, and the land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants (Leviticus 18:25), followed at once by the warning to Israel that it would do the same to her — that the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that were before you (Leviticus 18:28). The threat was kept in 586 BC.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines VOMIT as matter ejected from the stomach, and as a verb, to eject the contents of the stomach; he cites the scriptural proverb of the dog directly, the phrase having long been current in English.

expand to see more

VOMIT, n. — Matter ejected from the stomach; also, an emetic, a medicine that excites vomiting.

VOMIT, v.i. — To eject the contents of the stomach by the mouth.

VOMIT, v.t. — To throw up; to eject from the stomach; and figuratively, to throw out with violence.

The Authorized Version’s spue (Leviticus 18:28; Revelation 3:16) is the older English form of the same idea.

Revelation 3:16 applies the figure to a church rather than a land: because thou art lukewarm… I will spue thee out of my mouth.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 26:11 — "As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly."

2 Peter 2:22 — "But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire."

Leviticus 18:25 — "And the land is defiled: therefore I do visit the iniquity thereof upon it, and the land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants."

Leviticus 18:28 — "That the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that were before you."

Revelation 3:16 — "So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth."

Modern Corruption

2 Peter 2:22 is used on both sides of the perseverance debate; read with its own figures it settles the question, because a dog and a sow that return to type were never anything else.

expand to see more

The Arminian reading takes the chapter as proof that a saved man may be lost, since these had escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. The figures Peter chose decide it. He does not say the sheep went back to the mire; he says the sow did, after being washed. He does not say a son returned to the vomit; he says the dog did. Washing changed the sow’s outside and not her appetite, and that is precisely the doctrine of regeneration stated from the negative side: what these men lacked was a new nature. John says the same of the same class — they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us. Peter’s chapter is an argument for the necessity of the new birth, not against the security of the born again.

Leviticus 18 must not be softened either, and it is the passage that shows the conquest was moral rather than tribal. The land is said to vomit out its inhabitants for the abominations catalogued in the chapter — incest, adultery, child sacrifice to Molech, sodomy, and bestiality — and then Israel is told, in the same paragraph, that it will do the same to her for the same things. God did not have a lower standard for His own people. Revelation 3:16 applies the identical figure to a church that had grown comfortable, and the Laodicean sentence is the one the modern Western church should read first: not cold, not hot, and nauseating to Christ for that reason.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qi (H6892), vomit, and qo (H6958), to vomit or spue; Greek exerama (G1829), vomit, and emeo (G1692), to spue out, at Revelation 3:16.

expand to see more

Hebrew qo (H6958) — to vomit, to spue out; Leviticus 18:25, 28, and Jonah 2:10 of the fish.

Hebrew qi (H6892) — vomit, the matter itself; Proverbs 26:11, Isaiah 28:8.

Greek exerama (G1829) — vomit; a hapax legomenon at 2 Peter 2:22.

Greek emeo (G1692) — to vomit, to spue; only at Revelation 3:16, of the Laodicean church.

Greek kulisma (G2946) — a wallowing place, a mire; the sow’s return in the same verse.

Usage

"As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly (Proverbs 26:11) — nature unchanged, behaviour repeating."

"The land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants (Leviticus 18:25) — the moral ground of the conquest."

"I will spue thee out of my mouth (Revelation 3:16) — the same figure turned on a church."
